title: Liquid AI opens six-model LFM3 family at 2B parameters and 256K context
subtitle: The 2B-class family spans text, vision-plus-video, speech-to-speech, omni and decision models on one shared backbone, ships with open weights on Hugging Face, and runs the text model in roughly 1 GB at 4-bit precision for on-device use.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Liquid AI released LFM3 on October 27 as a family of six open-weight 2B-class models sharing a single backbone. The lineup covers text (LFM3-1.7B), vision with native video input sampled at 2 fps (LFM3-VL-2B), speech-to-speech across 18 languages with tool calling (LFM3-Audio-2B), an omni model that handles vision, audio and language together (LFM3-Omni-2B), and two decision models (d1-2B and d1-Omni-2B) that answer many questions in one forward pass. The text model has 1.73B parameters, a 256K-token context window, and support for 16 languages. Liquid says LFM3-1.7B outperforms its predecessor LFM2.5-2.6B with 35% fewer parameters, and the text model fits in roughly 1 GB of memory at 4-bit — small enough to run on phones and laptops. Weights are available on Hugging Face under the LFM Open License v1.0, and the models are also exposed through the Liquid AI Playground and API. Day-zero partners include Ambarella, AMD, Arm, Intel, Nvidia, OpenRouter, Qualcomm, and Vercel.

The shared-backbone architecture is the technical move worth paying attention to. Most multimodal families stitch a text model to separately trained vision and audio encoders, which multiplies the parameter count and complicates deployment. LFM3 trains one backbone and specializes it per modality, which is the same bet behind the recent generation of omni models from larger labs — but at 2 billion parameters instead of hundreds of billions. The result, if the benchmarks hold up on independent evaluation, is a set of models that fit the deployment envelope of edge devices without giving up the semantic richness of a multimodal system. The decision models are the most unusual piece: they are designed to answer a batch of related questions in a single forward pass, which cuts latency on applications like structured extraction and policy evaluation.

The release lands in a crowded small-model week. Meta's Muse family, Mistral's 3B series, Google's Gemma line, Microsoft's Phi models, and the Chinese open-weight releases from Moonshot, DeepSeek, and Zhipu have all converged on the sub-3B range as the deployment sweet spot. What distinguishes LFM3 is the modality coverage — six models under one license, with video and speech-to-speech included at the same parameter class as the text model, rather than offered later as separate releases. The license caveat matters: commercial use above a revenue threshold requires a paid enterprise license, so this is open-weight for research and small deployments and gated above a certain scale.

A note for learners: on-device AI is one of the practical frontiers that will decide where this technology actually gets used. A model that lives on a phone has latency, cost, and privacy properties no cloud model can match. If you want to build something useful with AI in the next twelve months and you don't need frontier reasoning, start with a 1–3B open-weight model from one of this generation of families — LFM3, Phi, Gemma, Qwen — and run it locally. The engineering discipline of fitting a real application into 1–2 GB of memory with a 256K context window will teach you more about model economics than any amount of API work with a 400B-parameter frontier model, because every token you spend is one you have to justify in the device budget.
